description: One reconstructed Proto-Indo-European word each week, with selected descendants, a compact family tree, and a deliberately tiny teaching sentence.
weather: Comparative skies are mostly clear; reconstruction remains reconstruction.

entries.lede: A small reconstructed root with a large carrying capacity: bears, burdens, transfers, and a Greek verb all travel in its family.

kerfuffle.note: One endures a burden; the other carries a chemical signal. Both still have an old idea of carrying tucked into their histories.

sentence.note: A deliberately schematic teaching reconstruction. PIE is not directly attested, and specialists may prefer different inflectional or accentual details.

entries.weather: Strong cognate front, with a light shower of aspirated stops.
entries.source_note: The root and family are reconstructions supported by comparison, not a written PIE dictionary entry. The diagram selects a few routes and leaves many relatives at home.

entries.lede: One of the easiest ancient family resemblances to taste: English eat and Latin-derived edible still sit close to the same table.

kerfuffle.note: One does the eating; the other merely passes the eligibility test. The disagreement is grammatical rather than gastronomic.

sentence.note: A compact pedagogical reconstruction, not an attested quotation. The spelling exposes a reconstructed laryngeal that would not have survived unchanged in the daughters.

entries.source_note: The reconstruction and selected reflexes follow comparative entries; exact ablaut grades and verbal formations deserve more space than a snack-sized page permits.

entries.lede: Stand, state, station, and static look busy now, but their older family occupation was simply staying upright.

kerfuffle.note: A bodily posture and an abstract condition both kept a notion of standing, then found very different jobs.

sentence.note: A teaching reconstruction. The root’s formations and the development of *-st- words involve more than one morphological route.

entries.source_note: The diagram groups familiar descendants by selected historical routes; sharing the root does not mean each modern word descended directly from the bare form shown above.

entries.lede: Vision, video, wit, wisdom, and the Vedas share this root, whose descendants include words for both seeing and knowing.

kerfuffle.note: One asks you to see; the other claims to know. The old semantic bridge ran from seeing to knowing.

sentence.note: A schematic teaching sentence. Case shape, verbal stem, and accent are simplified choices rather than a claim of a uniquely recoverable sentence.

entries.weather: Visibility excellent; semantics gradually changing from sight to knowledge.
entries.source_note: The semantic bridge from seeing to knowing recurs across the family. Modern English loans such as video arrived through Latin rather than by uninterrupted English inheritance.

entries.lede: A very old way to be: is, est, estí, and ásti preserve a striking family resemblance across several branches.

kerfuffle.note: This week’s kerfuffle is a peace conference: the forms travelled widely while the basic meaning barely budged.

sentence.note: A minimal teaching reconstruction. English needs an added ‘there’ to make the bare existential reading sound natural.

entries.source_note: Suppletive verbs such as ‘be’ collect forms from several roots. This page follows only the *h₁es- portion of that larger story.

entries.lede: Kin, kind, genus, generate, and genealogy spread from a root concerned with birth and coming into being.

kerfuffle.note: One names the people produced; the other names producing. A noun and a verb are disputing who owns the family paperwork.

sentence.note: A pedagogical reconstruction. Verbal stem formation is shown schematically, and the sentence is not directly attested.

entries.source_note: The modern English examples include inherited Germanic vocabulary and learned borrowings from Latin and Greek; the diagram keeps those routes separate.

entries.lede: Star, stellar, and asteroid are branches of one old night-sky word, though each arrived in English by a different route.

kerfuffle.note: One is a star; the other was named for looking star-like. Astronomy has since made the distinction rather firmer.

sentence.note: A tiny teaching reconstruction. It is designed to expose two familiar reconstructed forms, not to simulate an inscription.

entries.weather: Clear night, excellent comparative visibility, occasional initial laryngeal.
entries.source_note: The initial *h₂ is reconstructed from comparison and colouring effects; it is not a letter found in a PIE manuscript.

entries.lede: Water is old enough to have cousins from Hittite wātar to Greek húdōr and Slavic voda.

kerfuffle.note: One fills the pipe; the other describes what the pipe and its pressure can do. Same wet ancestry, different engineering duties.

sentence.note: A pedagogical existential. The syllabic *r̥ and reconstructed laryngeal are visible because this is a comparative form, not a normalized learner language.

entries.source_note: The noun had alternating stem shapes in the parent language. A single display form is convenient, but it does not replace the paradigm.

entries.lede: Mother, māter, mḗtēr, and mātṛ make one of the most recognisable kinship sets in the Indo-European family.

kerfuffle.note: A parent and a very large city meet because metropolis began as a ‘mother-city’, not because cities have opinions about bedtime.

sentence.note: A teaching reconstruction combining two familiar lexical items. It illustrates morphology without claiming a recoverable original utterance.

entries.source_note: Kin terms are old and morphologically irregular. The nominative display form is only one member of a reconstructed paradigm.

entries.lede: Father, pater, patḗr, and pitṛ are close relatives whose sound changes became textbook examples.

kerfuffle.note: One is a relationship; the other accumulated authority. The extra hierarchy arrived along the Greek route.

sentence.note: A schematic teaching reconstruction. The English translation is intentionally as small as the original.

entries.source_note: The Germanic form reflects regular sound changes rather than random drift; the diagram does not attempt to teach the full sequence.

entries.lede: New, novel, innovation, neo-, and Sanskrit náva share an old adjective that has spent millennia announcing fresh things.

kerfuffle.note: Novel began by announcing newness, then also became a whole kind of book. New would like its adjective back.

sentence.note: A playful teaching reconstruction. Predicate adjective syntax and word order are simplified for a first encounter.

entries.weather: A fresh lexical breeze, despite the root’s considerable age.
entries.source_note: Some English examples are inherited, while others are later learned or Romance loans. Their shared ancestry does not make their routes identical.

entries.lede: Rex, regal, raj, and Celtic -rix belong to a political word family whose routes through English are anything but direct.

kerfuffle.note: One became an adjective of kingship; the other names rule or a realm. Their shared history crossed very different empires.

sentence.note: A minimal teaching reconstruction. The displayed nominative belongs to a larger, irregular paradigm.

entries.source_note: Political titles travel through inheritance, borrowing, and name formation. The family relation is ancient; each English arrival has its own date and route.

entries.lede: Latin equus and Old English eoh name the same animal through different branches of the family.

kerfuffle.note: Latin keeps a stop where the Germanic branch developed a fricative. The resemblance becomes clearer when the intermediate forms are shown.

sentence.note: A pedagogical reconstruction using the thematic noun and a present form of *bʰer-. The asterisks mark reconstructed words; the clause is newly assembled.

entries.source_note: This selective diagram uses the conventional o-stem reconstruction. The initial laryngeal and the relation to Anatolian u-stems remain debated; the proposed derivation from a word for speed is not assumed here.

entries.lede: A tree can supply both a family diagram and a spear shaft: English tree and Greek dóru preserve different uses of the same material.

kerfuffle.note: One word readily suggests a living plant; the Greek cousin can name a weapon made from its wood.

sentence.note: A pedagogical reconstruction with a neuter nominative and an existential reading of *h₁ésti. It illustrates a possible clause, not a recovered utterance.

entries.source_note: The diagram selects two branches. English continues a formation built on the oblique stem *dréw-, rather than a simple sound-by-sound continuation of the displayed nominative *dóru.

entries.pronunciation: approximately ‘h₁-nóm-n̥’ · reconstructed neuter noun; final n is syllabic
entries.lede: English name and Latin nōmen belong together, even though scholars disagree about several details of their reconstructed ancestor.

kerfuffle.note: English inherited its word through Germanic. Latin supplies a cousin, not the source of the everyday English noun.

sentence.note: A pedagogical reconstruction that uses one conventional nominative. Neither this sentence nor its precise pronunciation is directly attested.

entries.source_note: This selective family tree groups related formations, not an agreed sequence of identical inflections. Reconstructions differ over laryngeals, vowel length and the paradigm; the Germanic noun is often connected with a collective formation.

entries.pronunciation: reconstructed *pṓds · long accented vowel · masculine root noun
entries.lede: English foot and Latin pēs put different consonants forward, but comparative evidence places them in the same family.

kerfuffle.note: English inherited foot through Germanic; Latin pēs is its cousin, not its donor.

sentence.note: A pedagogical reconstruction pairing the nominative with an existential verb. The English article and there make the tiny clause idiomatic; they are not extra reconstructed words.

entries.source_note: This selective diagram groups members of an alternating paradigm: the displayed nominative has a long vowel, while the oblique stem is *ped-. The Italic reconstruction *pets also has a published alternative, *pōts; the diagram follows the linked entry’s convention.

entries.pronunciation: reconstructed *ḱḗr · palatal stop and long accented vowel · neuter noun
entries.lede: A missing d in the headword is not a missing relative: the wider paradigm helps connect English heart with Latin cor, cordis.

lineages.branch: Germanic, with a remodeled noun stem

kerfuffle.note: The Latin genitive cordis makes the d visible. Compare the whole paradigm before judging the short nominative cor.

sentence.note: A pedagogical reconstruction, newly assembled to show a neuter subject. The accent and laryngeal notation represent scholarly analysis, not a surviving written sentence.

entries.source_note: Only the Germanic and Italic branches are selected. The reconstructed nominative *ḱḗr contrasts with the oblique stem *ḱr̥d-; Germanic also remodeled the noun as an n-stem. The connecting lines therefore summarize related formations, not unchanged inflections.

entries.pronunciation: reconstructed *ḱwṓ · palatal stop, w and long accented vowel · masculine noun
entries.lede: Before hound narrowed toward hunting dogs, its English ancestors could name a dog in general. Greek kýōn belongs to the same older family.

lineages.gloss: dog; now especially a hunting dog

kerfuffle.note: Greek keeps a k sound where the Germanic branch has h. The Germanic word also contains an added suffix, so the comparison is more than a letter swap.

sentence.note: A newly assembled pedagogical reconstruction using a thematic present of *bʰer-. What the dog carries is left unstated; the clause illustrates the subject and verb rather than reconstructing a particular ancient scene.

entries.source_note: The diagram selects the hound and Greek routes. Germanic continues a suffixed formation, cited as *ḱun-tós or *ḱwn̥tós. The displayed nominative *ḱwṓ is one scholarly convention; alternatives retain a final *n. Greek restored its final n by analogy within the paradigm.

sources.title: Wiktionary: hound, history and semantic narrowing
